The source prints Module 1 plus both an easy and a hard second module for each section; this set uses Module 1 and the HARD Module 2 of both sections (the easy second modules are not included). Figures and tables are cropped from the source PDF with its watermark removed; Math Module 1 Q5's four table choices are images. "Note: Figure not drawn to scale" captions that printed as broken glyphs (Math Module 2 Q1) are given as text in the question. Rationales and explanations were written for BlueMind. One source key corrected: R&W Module 2 Q26 (farm-size transition notes) prints D, but D states a claim about Thailand without the supporting evidence the goal requires; B makes the claim and supports it with Promkhambut et al.'s finding, so the key is B.

questions.passageText: Scientists have used machine learning tools to study elephant sounds, uncovering a sophisticated communication system. The tools ______ unique patterns in the rumbling sounds elephants make. The scientists claim that these patterns are specific calls the elephants use for individuals, similar to names.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.rationale: The tools were used to study existing elephant sounds, so they "detected" (discovered) patterns that were already there.
questions.explanation: The text says the machine learning tools were used to study elephant sounds and uncovered a communication system; the patterns are calls the elephants themselves use. So the tools found, or detected, patterns in the sounds, choice C. Choice A is wrong because the tools did not create the patterns—the elephants made the sounds. Choice B is wrong because nothing was being fixed; the tools analyzed the sounds rather than correcting them. Choice D is illogical: tools that scattered patterns would make them harder to find, not uncover them.

questions.passageText:
The following text is from Chinua Achebe's 1964 novel *Arrow of God*. The novel is set in Nigeria in the 1920s. Ezeulu, who is the religious leader for several villages, announces when the annual yam harvest can begin.

Whenever Ezeulu __considered__ the immensity of his power over the year and the crops and, therefore, over the people he wondered if it was real. It was true he named the day for the feast of the Pumpkin Leaves and for the New Yam feast; but he did not choose it. He was merely a watchman. His power was no more than the power of a child over a goat that was said to be his.
questions.questionText: As used in the text, what does the word "considered" most nearly mean?
questions.rationale: Ezeulu thinks carefully about the extent of his power and then wonders whether it is real, so "considered" means pondered.
questions.explanation: Whenever Ezeulu "considered" the immensity of his power, he "wondered if it was real" and reflected that he was merely a watchman. This is someone thinking deeply about a matter, so "considered" most nearly means pondered, choice A. Choice B is wrong because his power already exists; he is not looking forward to it. Choice C is wrong because "allowed" (permitted) makes no sense with "the immensity of his power" as an object here. Choice D is wrong because the passage shows him doubting his power, not showing esteem for it.

questions.passageText:
The following text is adapted from John Matheus's 1925 short story "Fog."

The fog extended its tentacles over city and river, gradually obliterating __traces__ of familiar landscapes. At five-thirty the old Panhandle bridge, supported by massive sandstone pillars, stalwart, as when erected fifty years before to serve a generation now passed behind the portals of life, had become a spectral outline against the sky.
questions.questionText: As used in the text, what does the word "traces" most nearly mean?
questions.rationale: The fog gradually hides the visible signs of the familiar landscape, so "traces" means indications.
questions.explanation: The fog spreads over the city and river and gradually wipes out what can be seen of the familiar landscape—even the bridge becomes only a "spectral outline." The "traces" being obliterated are the visible signs, or indications, of the landscape, choice C. Choice A is wrong because "debris" means scattered rubbish or wreckage, which the landscape is not. Choice B is wrong because the fog hides the real landscape, not copies of it. Choice D is wrong because the fog blocks what can physically be seen; it does not erase memories.

questions.passageText: Microplastics are a common pollutant in large masses of water like glaciers. High concentrations and ______ among particles—variations in size, shape, and material—make it onerous to comprehensively classify the microplastics in a water sample, so Ojeda-Benítez et al. are exploring a device to help quickly and accurately identify certain characteristics.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.rationale: The dashes define the missing word as "variations in size, shape, and material," which are inconsistencies among the particles.
questions.explanation: The phrase set off by dashes explains the blank: the particles show "variations in size, shape, and material." Differences of that kind are inconsistencies, choice B, and they make classification onerous (burdensome). Choice A is wrong because "restraints" are limits or controls, not variations. Choice C is wrong because "incompatibilities" means the particles cannot work or exist together, which the text never suggests. Choice D is wrong because "disruptions" are interruptions, not differences in physical characteristics.

questions.passageText:
The following text is adapted from Henry James's 1881 novel *The Portrait of a Lady*.

Everything Osmond did was pose—pose so subtly considered that if one were not on the lookout one mistook it for impulse. Ralph had never met a man who lived so much in the land of __consideration__. His tastes, his studies, his accomplishments, his collections, were all for a purpose.
questions.questionText: As used in the text, what does the word "consideration" most nearly mean?
questions.rationale: Osmond's every act is a deliberate pose and everything he does is "for a purpose," so he lives in the land of calculation.
questions.explanation: Osmond's behavior is a carefully planned pose that only looks like impulse, and "his tastes, his studies, his accomplishments, his collections, were all for a purpose." Living in "the land of consideration" therefore means living by deliberate planning, or calculation, choice B. Choices A and D are wrong because "deference" and "courtesy" refer to respect or politeness toward others, but the text is about Osmond's self-interested scheming, not his treatment of others. Choice C is wrong because Osmond is the opposite of indecisive: everything he does is purposeful.

questions.passageText: Adult glass eels can be found off the coast of Maine, but the eels begin their lives in the Sargasso Sea, a biodiverse area in the North Atlantic Ocean where they are born and later return to breed. Though biologists believe they have identified the general area in the Sargasso Sea that is crucial to the endangered eels' survival, little is yet known about how the animals spawn there. Scientists believe that solving the mystery will lead to better conservation of glass eels and their habitat, __helping in turn to sustain several other species that rely on them as a food source__.
questions.questionText: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It presents a finding from a study that identifies the circumstances required to ensure the survival of glass eels.
It suggests that scientists are more concerned about other species than about glass eels' habitat.
It indicates that the benefit of understanding glass eels' spawning behavior extends beyond the eels.
It discusses a role that glass eels and other species serve in supporting the ecosystem of the Sargasso Sea.

questions.rationale: The underlined portion adds that conserving the eels would also help other species that eat them, so the benefit reaches beyond the eels.
questions.explanation: The sentence says that solving the spawning mystery will improve conservation of glass eels, and the underlined portion adds that this would "in turn" help sustain other species that rely on the eels as food. It thus extends the benefit of the research beyond the eels themselves, choice C. Choice A is wrong because the text says little is known about spawning; no study has identified what is required for survival. Choice B is wrong because the text never ranks scientists' concerns—the eels' conservation comes first. Choice D is wrong because the underlined portion is about other species depending on eels as food, not about how eels and those species support the Sargasso Sea ecosystem.

questions.passageText: Tomi Adeyemi's first published work, the inventive West African–inspired fantasy novel *Children of Blood and Bone*, has intriguing things to say about the relationship between identity and power. Adeyemi works in a decades-long tradition going back to writers such as Samuel Delany and Octavia Butler, who wove cultural elements of the Black diaspora into their science fiction and fantasy in a movement known as Afrofuturism. At its core, the movement is characterized by speculation, not just about distant futures or other planets but also about alternate versions of our shared past. Afrofuturism's meditations on authority reinvigorate the creative potential of fiction.
questions.questionText: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It notes the political stance of an author, compares that author's book to other earlier works, and then analyzes the influence of political events on the book.
It praises a newly published author, compares that author with others who might appear superficially similar, and then points out the features of that author's work that make it unique.
It introduces an intriguing debut work, contextualizes that work as part of an ongoing literary tradition, and then describes important themes of that tradition.
It summarizes a book, describes characteristics of the artistic movement of which the book is a part, and then points out the features the book shares with more widely read works.

questions.rationale: The text introduces Adeyemi's first novel, places it in the Afrofuturist tradition of Delany and Butler, and then describes that tradition's central concerns.
questions.explanation: The first sentence introduces Adeyemi's debut novel as inventive and intriguing. The second sentence places her in a "decades-long tradition" (Afrofuturism) going back to Delany and Butler. The last two sentences describe what characterizes that movement—speculation about futures and alternate pasts, and meditations on authority. That matches choice C. Choice A is wrong because the text mentions no political stance of Adeyemi and no political events. Choice B is wrong because Delany and Butler are presented as genuine predecessors, not as superficially similar writers, and the text never singles out what makes Adeyemi unique. Choice D is wrong because the text does not summarize the book's plot or compare it to more widely read works.

questions.passageText: Founded in 1904, the Hispanic Society of America showcases the arts and cultures of Spanish-speaking and Portuguese-speaking regions around the world, including Latin America. It is located in New York City and has more than 18,000 objects in its museum collection. Since 2000, a number of other institutions devoted to Latino cultures have opened in the United States. A notable example is LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes in Los Angeles. It focuses on Mexican American art and culture.
questions.questionText: Which statement about the Hispanic Society of America is best supported by the text?

choices.text: It is no longer located in New York City.
It is visited by more people than any other Latino cultural institution in the US.

questions.rationale: The text states directly that the Hispanic Society of America has more than 18,000 objects in its museum collection.
questions.explanation: The second sentence says the Hispanic Society "is located in New York City and has more than 18,000 objects in its museum collection," which is choice A. Choice B contradicts the text, which says it is located in New York City. Choice C contradicts the text, which says it was founded in 1904; it is the other institutions that opened after 2000. Choice D is unsupported because the text gives no visitor numbers for any institution.

questions.passageText: In a 2024 study, Corrine Walsh and colleagues examined whether the composition of soil microbial communities could affect plants' flavor chemistry. Whereas Baslam et al. (2011) showed that adding specific bacterial or fungal strains to soil can yield increased flavonoid content in spinach crops, Walsh and team applied intact microbial communities gathered from ecologically distinct settings across Colorado, including areas of ponderosa pine forest and irrigated pasture, to mustard plants and evaluated the flavor compounds in the plants' seeds. This ensured that the microbial conditions in their experiment would better reflect the variation and complexity of naturally occurring communities.
questions.questionText: Based on the text, what is the most likely reason Walsh and colleagues chose to avoid the method used in the spinach study?

choices.text: The composition of microorganisms in the soil in the spinach study may not have been representative of a naturally existing composition.
The microbial community in the soil from the spinach study affected plants' nutrition, not their flavor chemistry.
The microbial community in the soil from the spinach study likely included similar species to those in wild soils.
The diversity of species of microorganisms in the soil from the spinach study was already abnormally high before the researchers added further microorganisms.

questions.rationale: Walsh's team used intact natural communities so their conditions would "better reflect" natural ones, implying that adding specific strains, as in the spinach study, produced unnatural compositions.
questions.explanation: The spinach study added "specific bacterial or fungal strains" to soil. Walsh's team instead used intact communities from real ecosystems, which "ensured that the microbial conditions ... would better reflect the variation and complexity of naturally occurring communities." The implied reason for avoiding the spinach method is that a few added strains may not represent a natural microbial composition, choice A. Choice B is wrong because the text says the spinach study increased flavonoid content, and the text does not distinguish nutrition from flavor as Walsh's reason. Choice C is the opposite of the implied concern: if the spinach soil already resembled wild soils, there would be no reason to avoid the method. Choice D is unsupported; the text says nothing about the spinach soil's diversity being abnormally high.

questions.passageText: A student is writing a paper on the global rise of the home video game industry during the 1980s. The student is researching the relative popularity of various genres of console and computer games. Looking at the information in the table, the student finds that the games in the genres of ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.text: puzzle and sports sold nearly the same number of units.
platformer and education sold nearly the same number of units.
puzzle and platformer outsold the games in the other genres.
platformer and sports outsold the games in the other genres.

questions.rationale: The puzzle game (*Tetris*, 43,000,000) and the platformer (*Super Mario Brothers 2*, 7,460,000) each sold more units than the education (4,000,000) and sports (2,420,000) games.
questions.explanation: The table lists units sold by genre: puzzle (*Tetris*) 43,000,000; platformer (*Super Mario Brothers 2*) 7,460,000; education (*Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego?*) 4,000,000; and sports (*Ice Hockey*) 2,420,000. The two top sellers are the puzzle and platformer games, so they outsold the other genres, choice C. Choice A is wrong because 43,000,000 and 2,420,000 are far apart. Choice B is wrong because 7,460,000 is nearly twice 4,000,000. Choice D is wrong because the sports game sold the fewest units of all.

questions.passageText: Wenhao Xu and colleagues demonstrated that applying a low direct current electrical field to graphite (a conductor) and an acrylamide (AAm) gel can increase how strongly materials adhere to each other. At some voltages, adhesion strength—as measured in kilopascals (kPa) of stress needed to pull the materials apart—was high (more than 30 kPa). But the mere application of a direct current electrical field with positive voltage is not sufficient to cause increased adhesion, as evidenced by the fact that ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.text: at 0 V, mean adhesion strength was equal to 0 kPa.
at 3 V, mean adhesion strength reached its highest observed level at approximately 30 kPa.
at 2 V, mean adhesion strength was lower than it was at both 1 V and 3 V.
at 1 V, mean adhesion strength was approximately equal to adhesion strength at 0 V.

questions.rationale: At 1 V (a positive voltage) adhesion strength stayed at about 8 kPa, the same as at 0 V, so applying a positive voltage did not by itself increase adhesion.
questions.explanation: The claim is that applying some positive voltage is not enough to increase adhesion. The graph shows about 8 kPa at 0 V and still about 8 kPa at 1 V; only at 2 V (about 15 kPa) and 3 V (about 40 kPa) does adhesion rise. So a positive voltage of 1 V produced no increase, choice D. Choice A misreads the graph—adhesion at 0 V was about 8 kPa, not 0—and a 0 V reading says nothing about positive voltage anyway. Choice B misreads the 3 V value (about 40 kPa, not 30) and in any case shows an increase, not the absence of one. Choice C is false: adhesion at 2 V (about 15 kPa) was higher than at 1 V.

questions.passageText: Working in Ghana, Emmanuel Hanyabui and colleagues compared the impact on pineapple growth of different combinations of soil additives, including NPK fertilizer (an inorganic fertilizer containing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium), organic compost, and biochar (a carbon-rich material produced from organic waste matter). Based on data in the table, pineapple farmers with no access to inorganic soil additives would likely increase the weight and size of their fruits by the greatest amount by using ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
questions.rationale: Without NPK (the only inorganic additive), the best treatment is biochar and compost: 979.3 g, 6.76 cm long, 13.68 cm in diameter—the largest values among the organic options.
questions.explanation: Farmers with no access to inorganic additives cannot use NPK fertilizer, so only control, biochar, compost, and biochar and compost are options. Among these, biochar and compost gives the greatest weight (979.3 grams), length (6.76 cm), and diameter (13.68 cm), choice C. Choice A is wrong because compost alone gives only 864.8 grams and actually reduces diameter (13.22 cm). Choice B is wrong because biochar alone (915.7 grams, 6.56 cm, 13.63 cm) is smaller on every measure than biochar and compost. Choice D gives the largest fruit overall, but NPK fertilizer is inorganic, so these farmers could not use it.

questions.passageText: Neuroscientist Artin Arshamian and his team sought to determine what affects a person's perception of an odor as pleasant: is it culture, personal taste, or aspects of human anatomy? The team assessed odor preferences in ten groups of people with different modes of living (urban, agricultural, and hunter-gatherer) including urban dwellers from a large city in Thailand and the Seri people from a small community in Mexico. The team observed that across cultures, people generally rated odors about the same: vanillin, which smells like vanilla, was typically rated more pleasant than galbazine, which smells like peanuts. The team therefore concluded that ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: culture likely plays more of a role in a person's perception of how pleasant an odor is than does human anatomy.
a person's mode of living likely doesn't have a large influence on that person's perception of whether an odor is pleasant or unpleasant.
a person who lives in an urban area is more likely to encounter the odor of vanillin than is a person who lives in a small community.
a person who perceives certain odors as pleasant will likely perceive the odors as roughly equal in pleasantness.

questions.rationale: Groups with very different modes of living rated odors about the same, so mode of living likely has little influence on odor pleasantness.
questions.explanation: The study compared groups with different modes of living (urban, agricultural, hunter-gatherer) and found that they "generally rated odors about the same." If such different lifestyles produce the same ratings, mode of living probably doesn't strongly shape odor perception, choice B. Choice A is the opposite of what the results suggest: similar ratings across cultures point away from culture and toward shared factors such as anatomy. Choice C is about exposure to vanillin, which the study did not measure. Choice D contradicts the findings: people rated vanillin as more pleasant than galbazine, so they did not see the odors as roughly equal.

questions.passageText: Outi Tervo and team studied the effect of human-caused noise on narwhals (*Monodon monoceros*), arctic marine mammals that are sensitive to acoustic changes in their environment. Hypothesizing that elevated sound levels affect foraging among narwhals, Tervo's team compared narwhal diving behaviors in natural sound conditions with those behaviors in two human-caused sound exposure conditions—ship sounds and ship sounds coupled with sonic pulses. Both exposure conditions resulted in significant decreases in the number and target depth of deep dives (associated with foraging) relative to natural conditions. However, differences between diving behaviors in the two exposure types were negligible, a finding that could be attributed to the fact that ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: sonic pulses can be heard at significantly greater ocean depths than ship sounds can.
ship sounds contribute so much to the overall sound level that the addition of sonic pulses has little effect on the narwhals' auditory environment.
narwhals forage at shallower depths in the presence of ship sounds alone than in the presence of ship sounds coupled with sonic pulses.
the narwhals weren't as sensitive to human-caused sounds as the researchers had predicted.

questions.rationale: If ship sounds already dominate the sound level, adding sonic pulses barely changes the environment, which explains why behavior was nearly the same in the two exposure conditions.
questions.explanation: The puzzle is why adding sonic pulses to ship sounds made almost no difference to diving behavior. If ship sounds already raise the overall sound level so much that sonic pulses add little, the two conditions would be acoustically similar for the narwhals, and their behavior would be similar too, choice B. Choice A would predict a difference between the conditions, since pulses would reach the narwhals in more places. Choice C describes a difference in foraging depth between the conditions, contradicting the finding that differences were negligible. Choice D contradicts the results: both exposure conditions significantly reduced deep dives, so the narwhals clearly were sensitive to the sounds.

questions.passageText: Jesse Treviño's 1976 painting *Mis Hermanos* was featured in the Smithsonian's 2013 exhibition *Our America: The Latino Presence in American Art*. The piece ______ chosen for the exhibition by curator E. Carmen Ramos.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: The painting was chosen before it was featured in the 2013 exhibition, a past event, so the past perfect "had been" is needed.
questions.explanation: The first sentence uses the past tense ("was featured" in 2013). The choosing happened before the painting was featured, so the past perfect "had been chosen" correctly places it earlier in the past, choice B. Choice A ("is") and choice D ("is being") are present tense, but the selection happened years ago. Choice C ("will be") is future tense, which is illogical for an exhibition that already took place in 2013.

questions.passageText: Mia Heavener's 2019 novel *Under Nushagak Bluff*, which takes place in a mid-twentieth-century rural Alaskan fishing ______ the story of three Yup'ik women who grapple with the rise of commercial fisheries and other changes affecting their community.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: The nonessential clause "which takes place ... village" opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "tells."
questions.explanation: The main sentence is "Mia Heavener's 2019 novel *Under Nushagak Bluff* ... tells the story." The clause "which takes place in a mid-twentieth-century rural Alaskan fishing village" interrupts it and begins with a comma, so it must end with a matching comma, choice C. Choice A is wrong because a colon cannot separate a subject from its verb. Choice B is wrong because the period leaves "Under Nushagak Bluff, which takes place ... village" as a fragment without a verb. Choice D is wrong because it leaves the nonessential clause unclosed.

questions.passageText: Many works of the Greek historian Strabo (1st century BCE) are ______ his *Geographica*, a descriptive history of the ancient world, is an extant work: it can still be read.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: "Many works ... are lost" and "his Geographica ... is an extant work" are independent clauses; a period separates them, and "Conversely" begins the second with a comma after it.
questions.explanation: Both parts are complete sentences: "Many works of the Greek historian Strabo ... are lost" and "his *Geographica* ... is an extant work." Choice A separates them with a period and sets off the transition "Conversely" with a comma. Choice B joins the clauses with "and" but no comma, and "conversely" lacks its proper punctuation. Choice C creates a comma splice—a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses, even with "conversely." Choice D is missing the comma after "conversely," which is needed before the subject of the second clause.

questions.passageText: Enacted in 1944, Iceland's 4,089-word constitution, in contrast to Spain's, which was enacted in 1978 and contains a far greater number (17,608) of words, ______ as the 2nd shortest in the world. Such data are studied by constitutional scholars like George Tsebelis, who can use them to draw broader conclusions.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: The subject is the singular "constitution" (Iceland's), so the verb must be the singular "ranks."
questions.explanation: Strip away the interrupting phrase "in contrast to Spain's, which was enacted in 1978 and contains ... words": the subject is "Iceland's 4,089-word constitution," which is singular. The verb must agree, so "ranks," choice D, is correct, and the present tense fits a current ranking. Choices A ("have ranked"), B ("rank"), and C ("are ranking") are all plural verbs that would agree with a plural subject, perhaps "words" in the interrupting phrase, not with "constitution."

questions.passageText: Working on an unimaginably small scale of billionths of a meter, nanoengineers have found ways to leverage cerium oxide ______ to improve treatments for certain conditions related to oxidative stress.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: The properties belong to many nanoparticles, so the plural possessive "nanoparticles'" is needed, and "properties" is a simple plural noun.
questions.explanation: The engineers leverage the properties of cerium oxide nanoparticles, so the possessive is needed on "nanoparticles," and since there are many particles it is the plural possessive "nanoparticles'." "Properties" possesses nothing, so it is a plain plural. That is choice C. Choice A wrongly makes "properties'" possessive, though nothing follows that it owns. Choice B omits the needed possessive apostrophe. Choice D uses the singular possessive "nanoparticle's," but the text refers to nanoparticles in general, not a single particle.

questions.passageText: Recordings of electrical activity in the brain, ______ increased activity in brain areas associated with suppressing motor functions.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: electrograms show that while responding to hypothetical match scenarios, the most highly skilled soccer players have
hypothetical match scenario responses show that the most highly skilled soccer players captured in electrograms have
the most highly skilled soccer players responding to hypothetical match scenarios have electrograms that show
responses to hypothetical match scenarios show that the most highly skilled soccer players have electrograms with

questions.rationale: "Recordings of electrical activity in the brain" is an appositive that must sit next to the noun it renames, "electrograms."
questions.explanation: The opening phrase "Recordings of electrical activity in the brain" is a descriptive noun phrase (an appositive), so the noun right after the comma must be what it describes. Electrograms are recordings of electrical activity in the brain, so choice A, which begins with "electrograms," is correct, and the rest of the choice completes the sentence logically. Choice B places "hypothetical match scenario responses" after the phrase, but responses are not recordings of brain activity. Choice C places "the most highly skilled soccer players" after it, illogically calling the players recordings. Choice D likewise makes "responses to hypothetical match scenarios" the thing described, which is incorrect.

questions.passageText: A team led by Portuguese researcher Isabel C.F.R. Ferreira found that many species of mushrooms contain chemicals called phenolic compounds, such as cinnamic acid and catechin. ______ Ferreira detected cinnamic acid in *Agaricus blazei* mushrooms and catechin in *Lentinus edodes* mushrooms.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.rationale: The second sentence gives specific mushroom species containing the compounds, illustrating the general finding, so "For example" fits.
questions.explanation: The first sentence states a general finding: many mushroom species contain phenolic compounds such as cinnamic acid and catechin. The second gives particular instances—cinnamic acid in *Agaricus blazei* and catechin in *Lentinus edodes*. Specific instances of a general claim call for "For example," choice D. Choice A signals a result, but detecting the compounds in two species is not caused by the general finding. Choices B and C signal contrast, but the second sentence supports the first rather than contradicting it.

questions.passageText: Resins play several important roles in maintaining the health of conifers and many other kinds of trees. ______ resins quickly seal wounds, which helps prevent harmful insects and fungi from entering trees. These sticky substances also help trees retain water that is needed for them to survive.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.rationale: Sealing wounds is one of the "several important roles" mentioned in the first sentence, so it is introduced as an example.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says resins play several important roles in tree health. The next sentences list specific roles—sealing wounds and helping retain water. The first of these is an illustration of the general claim, so "For example," choice D, is the logical transition. Choice A ("Regardless") suggests the information holds despite something just mentioned, which is not the case. Choice B ("Next") implies a sequence of steps or events, but the roles are not ordered in time. Choice C ("However") signals contrast, but sealing wounds supports the first sentence.

questions.passageText: While some researchers have identified the planet Kepler-296e as potentially habitable, it's unlikely that humanity will be able to take advantage of its favorable conditions anytime soon—it's 737 light years away. ______ humanity must first focus on making planets within our solar system more habitable.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.rationale: Because Kepler-296e is out of reach, humanity must focus on nearby planets in its place, so "Instead" fits.
questions.explanation: The first sentence explains that the distant Kepler-296e can't be used anytime soon. The second sentence offers an alternative focus: planets within our own solar system. A transition introducing an alternative is "Instead," choice B. Choice A ("Likewise") signals similarity, but focusing on nearby planets is not similar to Kepler-296e being too far away. Choice C ("For example") would make the second sentence an illustration of the first, which it is not. Choice D ("Next") implies the next step in a sequence, but the text presents the solar system as a replacement focus, not a later step after Kepler-296e.

questions.passageText: The Tres Zapotes archaeological site is located in our home state of Veracruz, Mexico. ______ an 8.5-ton stone statue of a human head was left behind by the ancient Olmec civilization. In the nearby state of Tabasco was another stone statue that weighs 19.8 tons.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.rationale: The statue was left at the Tres Zapotes site just mentioned, so "Here" logically refers back to that place.
questions.explanation: The first sentence names a place, the Tres Zapotes site, and the second tells what was found at that place: an 8.5-ton Olmec head. "Here" points back to the site, choice B; the contrast with "the nearby state of Tabasco" in the next sentence confirms that location is the focus. Choice A ("In other words") would introduce a restatement, but the statue is new information. Choice C ("Similarly") signals a comparison, but nothing comparable has been described yet. Choice D ("Therefore") signals a consequence, but the statue's presence is not a result of the site's location.

questions.passageText: In a 1948 article titled "The Language of Lines," Brazilian photographer José Yalenti argued that black-and-white photography's distinctive—and in his view, superior—use of lines is what elevates the medium to the status of fine art. ______ Yalenti insisted that conveying perspective through linear forms is photography's "indisputable and exclusive domain," creating a visual language surpassing even celebrated painters' works.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.rationale: The second sentence intensifies Yalenti's claim of photography's superiority, so the emphatic "Indeed" fits.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says Yalenti considered photography's use of lines superior and what makes it fine art. The second sentence goes further in the same direction—linear perspective is photography's "indisputable and exclusive domain," surpassing even celebrated painters. "Indeed," choice A, introduces such a reinforcing, stronger statement. Choice B ("In any case") dismisses what came before as unimportant, which doesn't fit a continuing argument. Choices C ("However") and D ("Even so") signal contrast or concession, but the second sentence agrees with and extends the first.

questions.passageText:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• A merchant ship is any ship hired to carry cargo or passengers.
• A ship's carrying capacity is also known as its deadweight tonnage (DWT).
• In 2021, there were a total of 1,323 merchant ships registered in the Bahamas.
• The combined DWT of these ships was 74.3 million tons.
questions.questionText: The student wants to emphasize the combined deadweight tonnage of the Bahamas' merchant ships in 2021. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: The carrying capacity of a merchant ship is also known as deadweight tonnage.
In 2021, the Bahamas had 1,323 merchant ships hired to carry cargo or passengers.
Combined, the Bahamas' merchant ships had a deadweight tonnage of 74.3 million tons in 2021.
There were a total of 1,323 merchant ships—ships hired to carry cargo or passengers—registered in the Bahamas in 2021.

questions.rationale: Only choice C states the combined deadweight tonnage (74.3 million tons) of the Bahamas' merchant ships in 2021.
questions.explanation: The goal is to emphasize the combined deadweight tonnage of the Bahamas' ships in 2021. Choice C states exactly that figure, 74.3 million tons, and leads with "Combined." Choice A only defines deadweight tonnage without giving the Bahamas' total. Choices B and D give the number of ships (1,323), not their combined tonnage.

questions.passageText:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Louis Ballard was a classical composer and citizen of the Quapaw Tribe.
• Ballard's composition *Desert Trilogy* was nominated for the Pulitzer Prize in music in 1971.
• His composition *Devil's Promenade* incorporates a Seneca cow-horn rattle, a traditional Native instrument.
• Ethnomusicologist Tara Browner claims that Ballard's compositions rely on elements originating within Native musical traditions.
questions.questionText: The student wants to support Browner's claim about Louis Ballard's compositions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.text: According to Browner, composer Louis Ballard, who wrote *Desert Trilogy*, relies on elements with origins in Native musical traditions.
Classical composer Louis Ballard, who wrote *Devil's Promenade*, was nominated for the Pulitzer Prize in music in 1971.
Browner posits that Louis Ballard's compositions rely on elements originating within Native musical traditions; *Devil's Promenade* affirms this assertion, incorporating a Seneca cow-horn rattle.
Browner claims that Louis Ballard's compositions, one of which was nominated for the Pulitzer Prize, rely on elements originating within Native musical traditions.

questions.rationale: Choice C states Browner's claim and supports it with evidence: *Devil's Promenade* uses a Seneca cow-horn rattle, a traditional Native instrument.
questions.explanation: To support Browner's claim that Ballard's music relies on Native musical elements, the student needs evidence of such an element in his work. The notes provide it: *Devil's Promenade* incorporates a Seneca cow-horn rattle, a traditional Native instrument. Choice C pairs the claim with that evidence. Choice A restates the claim but offers no supporting evidence, and *Desert Trilogy* isn't linked to any Native element in the notes. Choice B gives a Pulitzer nomination (and wrongly attributes it to *Devil's Promenade*), which says nothing about Native musical elements. Choice D restates the claim and adds the Pulitzer nomination, which does not support it.

questions.passageText: In the search for new impact craters on Mars, the roles of seismic monitoring and orbital imaging as data sources are ______: when vibrations detected with seismic monitoring indicate roughly where an impact has occurred, researchers can use orbital images of that relatively limited area of the rocky surface to precisely locate a new crater.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.rationale: Seismic data narrow the search to an area and orbital images then pinpoint the crater, so each method supplies what the other lacks: their roles are complementary.
questions.explanation: The colon introduces an explanation: seismic monitoring gives the rough location of an impact, and orbital imaging of that limited area gives the precise location. The two sources do different jobs that complete each other, so their roles are complementary, choice C. Choice A ("redundant") and choice D ("interchangeable") would mean the methods do the same job and either could replace the other, but the text shows them doing different, sequential tasks. Choice B ("exhaustive") means thorough and all-inclusive, which says nothing about how the two roles relate.

questions.passageText: Though copies of *The Adventures of Indiana Jones in Wenceslas Square in Prague on January 16, 1989*—an underground computer game that was created anonymously in 1989 as an act of political protest against the authoritarian regime of what was then Czechoslovakia—were originally distributed ______, the game is now readily available online for anyone to play.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.rationale: An anonymous, underground protest game under an authoritarian regime would have been distributed secretly, or surreptitiously, in contrast to its open availability today.
questions.explanation: The game was "underground," created "anonymously," and was a protest against an authoritarian regime, so it had to be shared in secret. "Though" sets up a contrast with today, when it is "readily available online for anyone to play." Secret distribution then versus open availability now calls for "surreptitiously," choice C. Choice A ("succinctly," briefly and clearly) describes speech or writing, not how copies are distributed. Choice B ("dispassionately," without emotion) doesn't fit a passionate protest and doesn't contrast with open availability. Choice D ("disingenuously," insincerely) implies deceitful intent toward recipients, which the text doesn't suggest.

questions.passageText: If some specific predictions in Alvin Toffler's 1970 book *Future Shock* seem ludicrous now—people do not wear paper clothing while living in underwater cities—Toffler's fundamental claim that rapid technological and social change will leave people feeling disoriented and atomized seems, in our age of disequilibrium and fragmentation, remarkably ______.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.rationale: Toffler's 1970 claim about disorientation and fragmentation matches today's "age of disequilibrium and fragmentation," so it seems remarkably prescient (it foresaw the future).
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts Toffler's specific predictions, which now seem ludicrous because they didn't come true, with his fundamental claim, which matches our current "age of disequilibrium and fragmentation." A prediction that turned out accurate is prescient, choice A. Choice B ("articulate") concerns how clearly the claim was expressed, not whether it came true. Choice C ("iconoclastic") means attacking established beliefs, which doesn't fit the contrast with the failed predictions. Choice D ("equivocal") means ambiguous or noncommittal, the opposite of a claim that now seems clearly borne out.

questions.passageText: A conclusive demonstration of the logical certainty of the honeycomb conjecture, posed in the first century BCE, ______ mathematicians' efforts until Thomas C. Hales presented the first valid proof of the conjecture in 1999.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.rationale: No one could prove the conjecture until Hales did in 1999, so a conclusive demonstration "defied" (resisted) mathematicians' efforts for centuries.
questions.explanation: The conjecture was posed in the first century BCE, but the first valid proof came only in 1999. For the intervening centuries, a proof resisted everyone's attempts—it defied their efforts, choice A. Choice B ("prefigured") means foreshadowed, which makes no sense: a proof didn't foreshadow mathematicians' efforts. Choice C ("epitomized") means was a perfect example of, but a proof that didn't exist can't exemplify the efforts. Choice D ("displaced") means replaced or pushed aside, which doesn't describe a proof that simply couldn't be achieved.

questions.passageText: Establishing protected areas (PAs), such as Abrolhos Marine Park in Brazil, is a common conservation strategy, but because PAs restrict some kinds of economic activity, it's widely thought that they hinder economic development. This perception is driven in part by the fact that economic assessments often don't capture the indirect effects of tourism linked to PAs. But Heng Zhu et al. found that tourism associated with Abrolhos boosts local demand for goods and services in other economic sectors, resulting in, for instance, increased income from fishing in nearby areas.
questions.questionText: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.text: It states a hypothesis that accounts for why PAs generally negatively impact local economies, outlines how a research team's findings support that hypothesis, and then suggests how a novel methodology led a separate team of researchers to a different conclusion.

It makes a generalization about the difficulty of using PAs to reconcile economic and conservation priorities, demonstrates why most PAs fall short of achieving that goal, and then holds up a particular PA as an example of how that goal can be achieved.

It introduces a widely held belief about the effect PAs have on the economy, proposes a reason for that belief's prevalence, and then details a study whose findings seemingly conflict with that belief.

It explains how PAs typically affect economic development in the regions where they are established, summarizes the findings of several economic studies that support this explanation, and then concedes that a particular PA is an exception to the general trend.

questions.rationale: The text presents the common view that PAs hinder development, explains that the view persists because assessments miss tourism's indirect effects, and then reports Zhu et al.'s contrary findings.
questions.explanation: Sentence 1 introduces a widely held belief ("it's widely thought" that PAs hinder economic development). Sentence 2 offers a reason the belief is common: assessments often miss tourism's indirect effects. Sentence 3 reports Zhu et al.'s finding that Abrolhos tourism boosts other sectors, which conflicts with the belief. That is choice C. Choice A is wrong because the text never says PAs do harm economies or that a research team supported such a hypothesis; there is only one study. Choice B is wrong because the text doesn't demonstrate that most PAs fail. Choice D is wrong because the text treats the negative effect as a perception, cites no supporting studies, and doesn't present Abrolhos as a mere exception.

questions.passageText: Most Native languages belong to language families, or groups of languages whose structural and lexical correspondence likely derives from their descent from a single language spoken long ago. A minority—such as Washoe, which is spoken in California and Nevada, and Chitimacha, which is spoken in Louisiana—are isolates, having no demonstrable genealogical relationship to other languages. __Yet Washoe and Chitimacha, like all isolates, are potentially remnants of families whose other members vanished before the historical record could attest to them, perhaps through the geographical expansion of extant families.__
questions.questionText: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.text: It implies that a nonisolate language may have influenced both Washoe and Chitimacha to such a degree that their relationship to their former families is no longer discernible.
It suggests that the ancestral languages of both Washoe and Chitimacha were likely isolates that replaced nonisolate languages through geographic expansion in the distant past.
It asserts that the historical record tends to overrepresent nonisolate languages relative to isolates, such that the origins of Washoe and Chitimacha are obscure to scholars in the present day.
It proposes that the distinction made between present-day nonisolate languages and isolates like Washoe and Chitimacha may not have been applicable in the distant past.

questions.rationale: The underlined sentence suggests that today's isolates may once have belonged to families whose other members disappeared, so the isolate/family distinction may not have held long ago.
questions.explanation: The first two sentences distinguish languages in families from isolates, which have no demonstrable relatives. The underlined sentence, introduced by "Yet," proposes that isolates like Washoe and Chitimacha may be the surviving members of families whose other languages vanished. In the distant past, then, these languages may not have been isolates at all, choice D. Choice A is wrong because the sentence attributes the lost relationship to other family members vanishing, not to influence from another language. Choice B reverses the scenario: the sentence suggests the expanding languages were extant families, not isolates. Choice C is wrong because the sentence says the other family members vanished before any record existed; it doesn't claim the record overrepresents nonisolates.

questions.passageText:
Text 1

Good art often challenges and disrupts social and aesthetic norms, but the creation of public art—paintings, sculptures, and performance pieces displayed in nonmuseum or nontheatrical public settings—typically requires broad agreement among artists, civic officials, and community members about the works' message and artistic goals. __Public art that fails to appease everyone by being sufficiently aesthetically and conceptually bland almost inevitably provokes backlash.__

Text 2

Public art is commonly displayed in spaces intended for purposes other than meaningful aesthetic engagement. Some critics of public art therefore note that norm-defying pieces that aren't effectively integrated within their surroundings in a manner that primes passersby to appreciate the pieces' merits (as is often the case) tend to be regarded more unfavorably than similarly provocative art encountered in museums is.
questions.questionText: Based on the texts, how would the critics mentioned in Text 2 most likely respond to the underlined claim in Text 1?

choices.text: By disputing the notion that civic leaders and community members are easily placated by art that is intended mainly to reinforce social norms
By agreeing with the idea that only works of art that are universally appealing are suitable for displaying in public spaces
By arguing that the reason members of the general public might disagree about a public artwork's merits is unrelated to the unconventionality of its appearance and ideas
By contending that the kinds of reactions controversial public artworks often receive aren't exclusively the result of attributes inherent in the works themselves

questions.rationale: The critics attribute negative reactions partly to how a piece is integrated into its setting, not just to its provocative content, so backlash isn't caused only by the work itself.
questions.explanation: Text 1 claims that public art that isn't bland enough to please everyone almost inevitably provokes backlash—locating the cause in the work's content. The critics in Text 2 note that provocative public pieces fare worse than similarly provocative museum art when they aren't integrated into their surroundings in a way that helps viewers appreciate them. So they would say the backlash depends partly on context and presentation, not only on qualities of the work, choice D. Choice A is wrong because the critics say nothing about how easily civic leaders are placated. Choice B is wrong because the critics suggest provocative art can succeed with proper integration; they don't endorse only universally appealing art. Choice C goes too far: the critics discuss "norm-defying" pieces, so they don't claim unconventionality is irrelevant—only that it isn't the whole story.

questions.passageText:
The following text is adapted from Mark Twain's 1876 novel *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer*. Aunt Polly is having dinner with Tom, her mischievous young nephew.

Aunt Polly asked [Tom] questions that were full of guile, and very deep—for she wanted to trap him into damaging revealments. Like many other simple-hearted souls, it was her pet vanity to believe she was endowed with a talent for dark and mysterious diplomacy, and she loved to contemplate her most transparent devices as marvels of low cunning.
questions.questionText: Which choice best describes how Aunt Polly is presented in the text?

choices.text: The narrator gently makes fun of Aunt Polly's mistaken confidence in her subtlety.
The narrator humorously exaggerates Aunt Polly's view of herself as an intellectual.
The narrator characterizes Aunt Polly as being excessively nosy about other people's private lives.
The narrator emphasizes that Aunt Polly's intentions are good even when she behaves impolitely.

questions.rationale: The narrator calls Aunt Polly "simple-hearted" and says she vainly sees her "most transparent devices" as "marvels of low cunning"—affectionate teasing of her misplaced belief in her own subtlety.
questions.explanation: Aunt Polly believes she has "a talent for dark and mysterious diplomacy," but the narrator calls this her "pet vanity," calls her "simple-hearted," and notes that her tricks are "transparent." The narrator is lightly mocking her mistaken confidence in her own cleverness and subtlety, choice A. Choice B is wrong because the text concerns her belief in her cunning and diplomacy, not her intellect in general. Choice C is wrong because she is questioning only Tom, her nephew, to catch him in mischief, not prying into other people's lives. Choice D is wrong because the text never comments on whether her intentions are good or her behavior impolite.

questions.passageText: From petroleum refining to fuel for residential heating, hydrogen has many applications. Currently, producing hydrogen is carbon intensive, but Alexandra M. Oliveira is one of many scholars investigating the feasibility of large-scale production of hydrogen through electrolysis, a process that emits no carbon when renewable energy is used. Oliveira suggests that although some obstacles may prevent electrolytic hydrogen from dominating energy systems, there is utility in its ability to decarbonize the petroleum and heating industries, where reducing carbon emissions is especially challenging.
questions.questionText: Which statement about the use of hydrogen in the petroleum and heating industries is most strongly supported by the text?

choices.text: The adoption of electrolytic hydrogen by these industries has been impeded by concerns about how carbon intensive its production is.
Development of applications for electrolytic hydrogen is less advanced in these industries than it is in most other carbon-intensive industries.
At least some of electrolytic hydrogen's potential to lessen these industries' carbon emissions is as yet unrealized.
The fact that large-scale electrolytic hydrogen production is not yet available has limited these industries' interest in pursuing hydrogen-based applications.

questions.rationale: Hydrogen production is currently carbon intensive and large-scale electrolysis is still being investigated, so electrolytic hydrogen's potential to decarbonize these industries has not yet been fully realized.
questions.explanation: The text says hydrogen production is currently carbon intensive and that scholars are still investigating whether large-scale electrolytic production is feasible. Oliveira points to electrolytic hydrogen's ability to decarbonize petroleum and heating—a potential benefit. Since the technology isn't yet operating at scale, at least some of that potential remains unrealized, choice C. Choice A is wrong because electrolytic hydrogen emits no carbon when renewable energy is used; it is current (non-electrolytic) production that is carbon intensive. Choice B is unsupported: the text compares these industries with no others in terms of development. Choice D is unsupported because the text says nothing about these industries' level of interest in hydrogen.

questions.passageText: In subtropical Asia, *Apis dorsata* (giant honeybee) plays an essential role in pollinating a wide variety of crops and wild plants. To study how different agricultural land covers affect the species, Rika Raffiudin and colleagues monitored the foraging activity of the bees as well as the pollen content of the honey from *A. dorsata* colonies at two sites in Indonesia: Kampar, characterized by its surrounding monoculture farms (growing a single crop), and Kerinci, a forest-agriculture site where multiple crops, including hot peppers and coffee, are grown nearby. The researchers concluded that a lack of crop variety may reduce total pollen collection by *A. dorsata*.
questions.questionText: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.text: Significantly fewer bees were observed engaging in foraging activities with the crops surrounding Kerinci than with the crops surrounding Kampar.
Honey samples from Kerinci bee colonies contained significantly higher concentrations of pollen than honey samples from Kampar bee colonies did.

Pollen in honey samples from Kampar bee colonies was predominantly sourced from a single plant species, whereas pollen in honey samples from Kerinci bee colonies was sourced from multiple different plant species.
In one Kerinci bee colony, a greater proportion of bees returned to their nests with pollen than returned without pollen, whereas the inverse was observed in a second Kerinci bee colony.

questions.rationale: More pollen in honey from the varied-crop site (Kerinci) than from the monoculture site (Kampar) shows that less crop variety goes with less pollen collected.
questions.explanation: The conclusion links crop variety to the amount of pollen collected: less variety, less pollen. Kampar has monoculture farms and Kerinci has multiple crops, so support would show more pollen collected at Kerinci. Choice B does exactly that: Kerinci honey had significantly higher pollen concentrations. Choice A would, if anything, suggest less pollen collection at the more varied site, weakening the conclusion. Choice C concerns the variety of pollen sources, not the total amount collected—an unsurprising result of the different crops that doesn't address quantity. Choice D compares two colonies within Kerinci with mixed results, so it says nothing about the effect of crop variety across sites.

questions.passageText: In 2009, the US state of Montana enacted rate stability regulations (RSRs), constraining insurance companies' latitude to raise premiums (the recurring fees policyholders pay to maintain insurance policies) once policies are in effect. Although RSRs are intended to benefit consumers, Naoki Aizawa and Ami Ko note that RSRs could curtail insurers' profits to such a degree that insurers abandon the market, thereby reducing the competitive pressure that typically restrains premium prices for newly issued policies. To determine whether this occurred in Montana, students first collect data on the number of insurers in the state for a few years leading up to and following 2009 and the premium prices for new policies offered by those insurers.
questions.questionText: Based on the text, what would be the most reasonable next step for the students to take to accomplish their goal?

choices.text: Compare changes over time in the premium price data the students have collected with changes over time in premium prices for policies that were already in effect during the same period in an otherwise similar state that had not enacted RSRs

Compare changes over time within each of the two types of data the students have collected with changes over time in analogous data for the same period from an otherwise similar state that had not enacted RSRs

Compare changes over time within each of the two types of data the students have collected with changes over time in the same types of data from Montana for a period beginning several years after 2009
Compare changes over time in the insurer-number data the students have collected with changes over time in insurer-number data from another state that enacted RSRs but not during the same period

questions.rationale: To isolate the effect of Montana's RSRs, the students should compare Montana's insurer counts and new-policy premiums over the same years with the same data from a similar state without RSRs.
questions.explanation: The students want to know whether Montana's 2009 RSRs drove insurers out and pushed up new-policy premiums. Changes in Montana alone could reflect nationwide trends, so they need a comparison group: a similar state without RSRs, observed over the same period, using the same two kinds of data (number of insurers and new-policy premiums). That is choice B. Choice A compares Montana's new-policy premiums with premiums for policies already in effect elsewhere—a different kind of data—and ignores insurer numbers. Choice C compares Montana with itself later on, which has no unaffected comparison group, since RSRs remain in place. Choice D compares only insurer numbers, and with a state whose RSRs came at a different time, so differing background conditions could explain any difference.

questions.passageText: Variously, researchers have closely examined obsidian artifacts to understand ancient social and economic structures, as in Raymond V. Sidrys's 1976 study, or to glean aspects of cultural identity, as in Dennis Ogburn and colleagues' 2009 study. Studies of the Malia archaeological site on the Mediterranean island of Crete have shown that significant changes to building styles—changes consistent with an influx of people from another culture elsewhere in the Mediterranean—occurred from the Middle Bronze Age to the Late Bronze Age. In a 2022 study, however, Tristan Carter and Vassilis Kilikoglou found that obsidian-object production methods at Malia stayed remarkably consistent during this architectural transition, which they interpret as indicative of local cultural continuity in the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.
questions.questionText: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Carter and Kilikoglou's argument?

choices.text: The obsidian used to produce objects at Malia was transported to Crete from the same source elsewhere in the Mediterranean throughout the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.
The methods used to produce obsidian objects at Malia during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages were also used by some other Mediterranean cultures in the period.
The obsidian-object production method that was most common among other Mediterranean cultures during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages was more efficient than the method used at Malia.
Changes to buildings like those that occurred at Malia have not been linked to changes in obsidian-object production methods in other Mediterranean cultures during the Middle and Late Bronze Ages.

questions.rationale: If other Mediterranean cultures used the same methods, newcomers could have kept producing obsidian the same way, so unchanged methods would not prove local continuity.
questions.explanation: Carter and Kilikoglou reason that because obsidian production methods didn't change, the local culture persisted despite the architectural evidence of an influx. That inference works only if newcomers would have brought different methods. If some other Mediterranean cultures used the same methods, choice B, then incoming people could have continued the same production, and consistent methods would no longer distinguish local continuity from cultural replacement. Choice A concerns the source of the raw material, not who was making the objects or how. Choice C, if anything, suggests newcomers would have switched to a more efficient method, so unchanged methods would better support continuity. Choice D suggests that architectural change and production-method change don't go together elsewhere either, which doesn't undermine their reading of Malia.

questions.passageText: The presence of other individuals of the same species has been observed to mitigate stress in highly social mammals. To investigate whether this phenomenon, known as social buffering, also occurs in reptiles, researchers led by Chelsea E. Martin monitored stress responses in wild southern Pacific rattlesnakes (*Crotalus helleri*) in three experimental treatments: when alone, with a rope, and with a companion *C. helleri*. The researchers compared the percent change between baseline and peak heart rate in response to a (harmless) disturbance, with higher values indicating higher stress levels.
questions.questionText: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the idea that social buffering occurs among *C. helleri*?

choices.text: Average peak heart rates were highest among solitary *C. helleri*, but no differences were observed in average peak heart rates between *C. helleri* with a companion and *C. helleri* with a rope.
*C. helleri* with a companion displayed a lower average baseline heart rate and lower average peak heart rate than did solitary *C. helleri* or *C. helleri* with a rope.
The average percent change in heart rate was lower among *C. helleri* with a companion than among solitary *C. helleri* and *C. helleri* with a rope.

Solitary *C. helleri* had higher average baseline heart rates than did *C. helleri* in the other treatments, but the average percent change in heart rate was smaller among solitary *C. helleri* than among *C. helleri* with a companion.

questions.rationale: Stress was measured as the percent change from baseline to peak heart rate; a lower value with a companion than when alone or with a rope shows another snake specifically reduced stress.
questions.explanation: The researchers' stress measure is the percent change between baseline and peak heart rate, with higher values meaning more stress. Social buffering means another member of the species reduces stress, and the rope treatment controls for simply having an object nearby. Choice C shows a lower percent change with a companion than both alone and with a rope, directly supporting social buffering. Choice A shows no difference between companion and rope, so the effect isn't specifically social, and it uses peak rates rather than the percent-change measure. Choice B reports baseline and peak rates separately, not the percent change the study used, so it doesn't establish a smaller stress response. Choice D shows a smaller stress response among solitary snakes, which contradicts social buffering.

questions.passageText: Mountain summits are often described in terms of their elevation, or height above sea level. But a summit's elevation may not be as good an indication of how high the mountain appears to observers as is the summit's prominence, or its height above its surroundings, and these values can differ significantly. For example, the Indian mountain of ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?

choices.text: Saser Kangri III has an elevation of 7,495 meters but a considerably lower prominence of 850 meters.
Kangto has a much higher prominence than does Langpo.
Kangto has a high prominence but is from a different mountain range than Mount Lakshmi, which has a lower prominence.
Sri Kailash has an elevation of 6,932 meters and is considered the highest mountain from the Garhwal Himalaya range.

questions.rationale: The example must show elevation and prominence differing significantly for one mountain; Saser Kangri III's elevation is 7,495 meters but its prominence is only 850 meters.
questions.explanation: The claim is that a summit's elevation and prominence "can differ significantly," so the example should give both values for a single mountain and show a large gap. Choice A does this: Saser Kangri III's elevation is 7,495 meters while its prominence is only 850 meters. Choice B compares the prominence of two different mountains and says nothing about elevation. Choice C mentions mountain ranges and prominence but no elevations, so it doesn't illustrate a difference between the two values. Choice D gives only Sri Kailash's elevation, not its prominence, and the claim that it is the highest in its range isn't in the table.

questions.passageText: Whereas Joan Lockard's 1984 study of captive gorillas reported more right-handedness than left-handedness, Jane Goodall's 1963 study of wild chimpanzees did not. According to a meta-analysis of studies of nonhuman primates, captive populations are more likely to be described as right-handed than wild populations are. Statistical analysis indicates a handedness study would need a minimum of 176 individuals to show a representative result; however, the study by Lockard included a total population of 8, and the study by Goodall included a total population of 8. This suggests that ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: neither the study by Lockard nor the study by Goodall provides sufficient evidence to make a meaningful comparison about handedness in primates.
the study by Lockard reliably represents handedness in captive primates, but the study by Goodall likely does not reliably represent handedness in wild primates.
Goodall likely underestimated the prevalence of right-handedness among the wild chimpanzees in the study.
the study by Lockard reliably represents handedness in captive primates but not in wild primates.

questions.rationale: Both studies had only 8 individuals, far below the 176 needed for a representative result, so neither supports a meaningful comparison.
questions.explanation: A representative handedness study needs at least 176 individuals, but both Lockard's and Goodall's studies had only 8. Neither study's result can be considered representative, so comparing them tells us little, choice A. Choices B and D claim that Lockard's study is reliable, but it is just as far below the 176-individual threshold as Goodall's. Choice C makes a specific claim about the direction of Goodall's error; a small sample makes a result unreliable but doesn't show that right-handedness was underestimated.

questions.passageText: Interested in how the color of dogs' irises affects human responses to dogs, Akitsugu Konno et al. showed images of 12 dogs' faces to human participants and asked them to rate the dogs' kindness and trustworthiness as well as the likelihood that they would interact with or keep the dogs. The researchers had previously adjusted the images so that each dog was presented in two versions, one with light irises and one with dark irises. They distributed the images such that no participant saw both the light and dark versions of the same dog. Konno et al. found that participants responded more positively to the latter. The study's design allowed the researchers to exclude the possibility that the results ______
questions.questionText: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.text: may have been different if participants had been able to see the dogs' irises in person instead of only seeing images that included the dogs' irises.
reflected a preference on the part of participants for facial features that happened to coincide with dark irises in the dogs depicted in the images.
were a function of participants emphasizing the colors of the dogs' irises over the dogs' kindness and trustworthiness when reacting to the images.
could be explained by participants having preexisting positive feelings about dogs with dark irises or preexisting negative feelings about dogs with light irises.

questions.rationale: Every dog appeared in both a light-iris and a dark-iris version, so all other facial features were identical across the two; the preference can't be due to other features that happened to accompany dark irises.
questions.explanation: Because each dog's image was edited into a light-iris version and a dark-iris version, the only difference between the two versions is iris color; every other facial feature is held constant. So the researchers can rule out that participants were really responding to other features that happened to occur in dark-eyed dogs, choice B. Choice A can't be excluded—the study used only images, so it can't tell us what in-person viewing would show. Choice C is not something the design addresses, and iris color was the very variable being tested. Choice D can't be excluded either: preexisting feelings about iris color would be consistent with, not ruled out by, the results.

questions.passageText: Growing as large as three meters in diameter, the leaves of the giant Amazonian waterlily feature a complex network of radiating veins that provide structural ______ in thickness from the center to the edges, these veins allow the leaves to maintain their large size and buoyancy with minimal material, optimizing light capture and photosynthesis.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: "Growing ... support" is a complete sentence, and "Decreasing ... these veins allow ..." is another, so a period is needed between them.
questions.explanation: The first sentence ends with "veins that provide structural support." The next sentence begins with the modifier "Decreasing in thickness from the center to the edges," which describes the subject "these veins," followed by the verb "allow." Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, so choice A is correct. Choices B and C join two independent clauses with only a comma (a comma splice); "while" in C turns the phrase into a modifier but still leaves "these veins allow ..." attached by just a comma. Choice D runs the sentences together with no punctuation.

questions.passageText: Charles Dickens's classic 1850 novel about a young man named David Copperfield has a title that is instantly recognizable to many readers: *David Copperfield*. Dickens's novel originally had a different ______ while writing and editing, Dickens had planned to call the novel *Mag's Diversions*.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.rationale: "Though" belongs to the first clause ("Dickens's novel originally had a different title, though"), and a semicolon then separates it from the second independent clause.
questions.explanation: Here "though" is a transitional adverb meaning "however" that contrasts this sentence with the previous one, so it belongs with the first clause: "Dickens's novel originally had a different title, though." The clause that follows, "while writing and editing, Dickens had planned to call the novel *Mag's Diversions*," is independent, so a semicolon must separate the two, choice A. Choices B and D join two independent clauses with only a comma (or no punctuation), creating a comma splice or run-on. Choice C attaches "though" to the second clause, producing "though while writing and editing, Dickens had planned..."—which makes the second clause subordinate and illogical.

questions.passageText: *On Guard* is a 1997 photograph by Iranian artist Shirin Neshat. Like many of Neshat's photos, the work features a pair of hands. Clasping a microphone, one hand ______ covered in Persian script, the hands imply an out-of-frame figure on the edge of speaking.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: is bare and the other is

questions.rationale: The material before "the hands imply" must be a verbless absolute phrase modifying the main clause: "one hand bare and the other covered in Persian script."
questions.explanation: The main clause is "the hands imply an out-of-frame figure on the edge of speaking." Everything before it must be a modifier, not a clause. Choice C creates the absolute phrase "one hand bare and the other covered in Persian script," with no finite verb, which correctly describes the hands. Choice A adds verbs ("is bare," "is covered"), creating independent clauses joined to the main clause by only a comma—a comma splice. Choice B makes "the other is covered" a clause, again creating a comma splice. Choice D makes "one hand is bare" a clause and joins it to the rest with only a comma.

questions.passageText: The exoplanet Pi Mensae d was discovered using an indirect approach to planetary detection, the radial velocity method. Compared to that of the direct imaging method, ______ the effect these exoplanets have on nearby stars.
questions.questionText: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.text: the detection of distant exoplanets, too dim to be observed in the radial velocity method's vast zone of discovery, is based on
the radial velocity method's zone of discovery is vast, as distant exoplanets too dim to be observed are detected by
the radial velocity method, with its vast zone of discovery, detects exoplanets that are too dim to be observed by
distant exoplanets too dim to be observed are detected within the radial velocity method's vast zone of discovery through

questions.rationale: "That of the direct imaging method" stands for "the direct imaging method's zone of discovery," so the subject being compared must be "the radial velocity method's zone of discovery."
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase "Compared to that of the direct imaging method" uses "that of" to stand for a noun, and the subject right after the comma must be the same kind of thing it is compared with. Only choice B supplies a matching subject: the radial velocity method's zone of discovery is compared with that (the zone of discovery) of the direct imaging method, and the rest of the sentence logically explains why it is vast. Choice A makes "the detection of distant exoplanets" the subject, which doesn't match "that of" and says the exoplanets are too dim to be observed within the radial velocity zone, contradicting the method's purpose.
